title: {{NAME}} and the Storm That Stole the Colours
moral: Gentleness is not weakness — it is often the most powerful force in any room.

pages.content:
The Prism Plains were named for exactly the thing that was now wrong with them: the colours were gone. Where yesterday every field had blazed with ten impossible shades and the air itself had tasted faintly of warm light, today everything wore only grey. The sky was the grey of old pewter. The grass was the grey of cold ash. Even the Diplodocus herds moving across the plain looked like walking shadows of themselves, their usually vivid hides bleached to the colour of quiet.

{{NAME}} landed at the edge of the plains with the purple cape folding around both feet, and immediately felt the wrongness as a pressure behind the eyes, the specific discomfort of a world from which something essential has been removed. The local guide, a young Ankylosaurus named Cobble, was waiting by a standing stone. He had been blue-green yesterday. Today he was the colour of a cloudy mirror.

The Prism Plains ran on colour, Cobble explained, in the methodical way that worried animals explain things. Not metaphorically: literally. The Chromavore Storm came every generation and drank the colour from the land. It could be driven off, but only if someone could reach the Storm's eye, where the collected colours sat in a spinning vortex, and return them. No one had managed it yet. The storm liked power and force. Both had been tried. Both had been absorbed.

pages.content:
The unicorn found {{NAME}} before {{NAME}} found the unicorn, which was her way.

Her name was Prism, which was either a very good coincidence or no coincidence at all, and she materialised from the grey morning mist like a rumour becoming fact. She was the last creature on the plains whose colour remained. Her coat was a deep, breathing gold, not bright but warm, like candlelight choosing to stand firm in a draughty room. Her horn rotated light into fragments that dropped to the grey grass and briefly remembered what green felt like.

{{NAME}}'s expression, later described by Cobble as 'extremely surprised and then immediately less surprised,' was exactly what happened when something you'd read about in briefings suddenly stood six feet away breathing warmly on your cape.

'The storm feeds on force,' Prism said. Her voice was the kind that carries weight without weight. 'Every hero who has tried to fight it has only made it bigger. The wind inside it is made of repurposed effort.' She tilted her luminous head. 'But gentleness confuses it. It has no template for tenderness. It simply doesn't know what to do.' {{NAME}} considered this carefully. It was the most counterintuitive tactical briefing ever received. It was also, in the way of such things, obviously correct.

pages.content:
They walked toward the storm together, which was different from charging at it. Walking instead of flying. Keeping the speed low and the intention quiet.

The Chromavore Storm was colossal close up, a spinning column of dark cloud that stretched from ground to sky and hummed with a high, hungry frequency. Around its edges, stolen colour swirled in trapped ribbons: emerald, violet, flame-orange, the specific blue of a summer sky at exactly two in the afternoon. The wind it produced should have knocked {{NAME}} backward. Instead it seemed uncertain, gusting in irregular pulses, as though searching for the threat it expected and couldn't locate.

Cobble bellowed from behind them: a long, low Ankylosaurus call that was the sound his species used to comfort frightened young ones. Not defiant. Not aggressive. Just warm. The storm flickered. A thread of colour, a brilliant crimson, uncoiled from its edge and drifted toward them like a sleeping ribbon waking up.

Prism stepped forward and let her golden light expand outward, not as a weapon but as an offering, the way a fire shares its warmth without asking for anything back. The storm's hum changed pitch, climbing toward something almost like confusion. {{NAME}} spread both arms wide, cape unfurling like a yellow flag, and simply stood: present, open, quiet. The antithesis of a threat. The storm had never encountered this before and it showed.

pages.content:
The moment when the Chromavore Storm broke was quiet rather than explosive, which was appropriate.

The hum dropped. The spinning slowed, like a top that has decided it's tired. The first colour to return was the specific green of new leaves, cascading outward from the storm's eye in a wave that raced across the plains faster than sight. Then cobalt blue, then amber, then a dozen more in rapid succession, pouring back into the world with the relief of water returning to a dry riverbed.

The storm itself didn't disappear. It became something smaller, something that fit in your hand: a small spinning spiral of cloud no bigger than a fist, hovering uncertainly in the air between {{NAME}} and Prism. It had lost its hunger. Without the stolen colours to feed it and without force to absorb, it was simply a small weather phenomenon looking for somewhere to be.

Prism touched it with the very tip of her horn. Gently. Like answering a question with a better question. The storm dissolved into a soft, harmless mist that settled over the plains like a first morning's dew, and wherever it landed the grass turned a shade richer than it had been even before.

Cobble had his colour back. He was an extraordinary blue-green, like the sea deciding to be a forest. He stared at his own feet with evident amazement.

pages.content:
The Prism Plains at sunset, with all their colours returned and then some, were genuinely hard to look at directly in the best possible way. Every shade seemed to have come back slightly more itself than before, as though the brief absence had reminded the world exactly what it was.

The Diplodocus herds moved across the restored plains in a river of warm terracotta and sage, their long necks swaying with the particular satisfaction of animals who have had a very unusual day and are pleased it has resolved. Cobble trundled beside {{NAME}} wearing his colours with the careful pride of something recovered and appreciated.

Prism stood at the crest of a low hill with the last sunlight making a ceremony of her gold, and looked at {{NAME}} with an expression that contained a whole conversation that didn't need words. {{NAME}} nodded once. She dipped her horn once. They understood each other.

{{NAME}} sat down in the restored grass, and it was soft and green and smelled like the world at its best. The purple cape spread around like a circle of calm. Every colour the eyes could hold was present in the sky above, doing what light does when it decides to be generous.

Rest now, bright one. Let the colours fill your dreams the way they fill this sky: without hurry, without fuss, in every shade at once. And somewhere in the plains tonight, a small harmless mist is drifting, and no one is quite sure what it will become.
